text: Describe how a binary search finds an item in a list.

mark_points.text: List must be sorted before the search begins
Compare the target with the middle item
Discard the half of the list that cannot contain the target
Repeat until the item is found or the search interval is empty

text: A sorted list contains [3, 8, 12, 21, 30, 45]. Trace a binary search for 21.

mark_points.text: Recognises that the list is already sorted
Starts by checking the middle item or one of the two central items
Chooses the correct half after comparison
Repeats the midpoint comparison in the remaining interval
Stops when 21 is found

text: Describe the main steps of bubble sort.

mark_points.text: Compare adjacent pairs of items
Swap adjacent items that are in the wrong order
Repeat passes through the list so larger items move to the end
Stop when a pass makes no swaps or the list is sorted

text: Explain why a recursive algorithm needs a base case.

mark_points.text: A recursive algorithm calls itself
A base case gives a condition where recursion stops
Each recursive call should move closer to the base case
Without a base case the algorithm may recurse forever or crash

text: State two edge cases for binary search and how the algorithm handles them.

mark_points.text: An empty list has no middle item to inspect
The algorithm should report not found when the interval is empty
The sorted precondition still applies for binary search
The loop or recursion terminates when the search range is empty
